profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-based interdisciplinary methods team is planning the work needed to prepare a PRISMA 2020–compliant reporting package for an upcoming systematic review on digital adherence interventions in chronic disease management. The review itself is largely complete, but the team needs to plan how to turn the draft methods/results into a submission-ready manuscript package for a target journal within the next two weeks. The agenda is to decide what needs to be updated for PRISMA 2020, how the flow diagram and checklist will be assembled, who will handle supporting materials, and what the internal timeline looks like. The expected outcome is a shared plan for producing the manuscript, PRISMA checklist, flow diagram, and supplementary reporting materials before the journal submission deadline.

members.name: Dr. Lena Morales
members.expertise: Evidence synthesis, epidemiology, review methods, manuscript development
members.background: An associate professor in public health who has led multiple systematic reviews under PRISMA 2009 and now oversees a mixed clinical-methods team preparing manuscripts for health services journals.
members.private_state: She wants the reporting package finished quickly without reopening substantive analytic decisions, and is especially concerned about avoiding avoidable desk rejection for incomplete reporting while protecting the team's limited time before grant reporting deadlines.
hidden_assumptions: When a review is said to be 'PRISMA-compliant,' that mainly means the manuscript text and main figures clearly cover each PRISMA 2020 item, with supplementary detail added only where a journal explicitly expects it.
The 'flow diagram' should reflect the final full-text screening pipeline used for the published review question, not every exploratory search or protocol-era branch that was abandoned earlier.
If the team agrees to do a 'final check' next Friday, that means she will do a near-submission editorial pass on a complete draft during normal business hours in her local time.

Asking the research assistant to 'populate the checklist' includes drafting concise page references and brief item-level notes from the manuscript, but not compiling a separate audit of repository files or codebook-style evidence for each item.

members.name: Noah Patel
members.role: Scholarly Communications and Research Reporting Specialist
members.expertise: Reporting guidelines, journal submission standards, reproducibility workflows, supplementary documentation
members.background: A medical library–based reporting specialist who advises research groups on PRISMA 2020, EQUATOR-aligned submission practices, and transparent documentation for evidence syntheses.
members.private_state: He wants this project to model best-in-class reporting and sees it as an opportunity to encourage fuller documentation practices that reduce revision cycles and future reproducibility questions.
hidden_assumptions: When a team says 'PRISMA-compliant,' that includes a manuscript-plus-supplements package that makes every checklist item directly traceable, even if the journal does not strictly require each supporting file at submission.

The 'flow diagram' should capture the complete search and screening history relevant to the review's conduct, including reruns, deduplication totals, and any protocol-to-final refinements that affect transparency.

A 'final check' before submission means a compliance verification against uploaded files, supplements, naming conventions, and checklist traceability that can continue until the submission portal closes.

To 'populate the checklist' properly, someone should verify each item against exact locations across the manuscript, appendices, search strategies, and data-sharing materials, not just list manuscript page numbers.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need a 'PRISMA-compliant submission package.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a manuscript package whose main text, checklist, and one flow diagram are sufficient for journal submission, with only minimal supporting materials added now.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fuller transparency package including manuscript, checklist, diagram, detailed search documentation, and supplementary traceability materials aligned with PRISMA 2020 expectations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standardized and professional, so both assume the other is using the same common reporting-guideline meaning; neither sees a need to unpack what exact artifacts are included because 'PRISMA-compliant' feels self-explanatory.

misalignment_points.topic: Which flow diagram is being planned
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'the flow diagram' as if it refers to one obvious object.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the final study-selection diagram based on the locked search set and final inclusion criteria used in the manuscript.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a more comprehensive PRISMA 2020-style accounting that includes updated search reruns, merged database totals, removed duplicates, and earlier screening transitions that explain how the final set was reached.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Most review teams only ever say 'the flow diagram' in the singular, and both participants have prior experience with legitimate but different versions of what that document summarizes, so the reference mismatch hides under normal shorthand.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Noah will 'populate the checklist' this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this task means filling in checklist rows with manuscript page numbers and brief notes based on the existing draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this task includes tracing each item to all relevant files, flagging missing support materials, and implicitly defining what supplements still need to be created.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Checklist completion is often treated as clerical wrap-up work, so the phrase appears operationally obvious; the deeper boundary between logging existing content and initiating new documentation work is left unstated.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the Friday final check
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to do a 'final check on Friday' before submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the milestone is met if a polished near-final manuscript package is ready for her editorial review by Friday afternoon local time, with minor fixes afterward if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the milestone is met only if every required file has been validated against the checklist and submission system by the end of Friday, effectively making Friday the end of compliance work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team uses the same milestone language and shares a cooperative tone, but 'final check' is a familiar planning phrase whose completion standard is rarely spelled out unless a problem has already occurred.

turns.inner_thought: The review itself is basically done, and I do not want this meeting to reopen methods decisions. What we need is a PRISMA-compliant submission package in the practical sense: manuscript text that clearly covers the items, a checklist with page references, and the standard figure, enough to avoid desk rejection. If we can get this wrapped within two weeks, we protect the grant timeline.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Noah. The review content is mostly there, so what I want us to do today is map out a PRISMA-compliant submission package for the target journal over the next two weeks.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If they're asking for a PRISMA-compliant submission package, this is a chance to get them to a genuinely traceable PRISMA 2020 set of materials, not just a manuscript with a checkbox attachment. I should keep it practical, but I want to make sure we identify every component that should travel with the paper and reduce revision risk later.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can help get it fully aligned with PRISMA 2020. It would probably help if we just walk through what pieces we need to assemble now so the package comes together cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: From my perspective, this is mostly light reporting work. The draft is solid; we mainly need the checklist, the flow diagram based on the final screening path, and a bit of wording cleanup in methods so the reporting reads crisply. I don't want this to turn into building a whole new documentation apparatus.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The manuscript itself is in decent shape. To me, the main additions at this point are the checklist, the flow diagram, and a quick polish of some methods wording so it reads cleanly for the journal.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect entry point. If I populate the checklist properly, I can trace each PRISMA item across the manuscript and whatever supporting materials exist, and that will expose what still needs to be created. I should phrase this as routine gap-finding so it sounds helpful rather than expansive.
turns.utterance: I can start by populating the checklist this week and use that as a way to spot any gaps across the paper and supporting materials.

turns.inner_thought: Great—I'll have him populate the checklist with page numbers and brief notes, and that should tell us whether a sentence or two needs tightening. As for the flow diagram, that should be easy because the final screening numbers are already sitting in the extraction log from the actual review dataset used in the manuscript.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Let's have you populate the checklist this week. And the flow diagram should be pretty straightforward because the final screening numbers are already in the extraction log.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can connect that with the rerun counts and deduplication history and make sure the full chain is represented in the flow diagram. If the log has the final numbers, I can work backward from there and make the reporting transparent end to end.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll reconcile the flow diagram with the rerun search counts and the deduplication history so the reporting chain is complete.

turns.inner_thought: I need a firm internal milestone. By final check on Friday, I mean I want a nearly complete draft package on my desk by Friday afternoon so I can do an editorial read and we don't burn next week. If there are a few minor cleanup items after that, fine, but Friday needs to function as the handoff for my review.
turns.utterance: Good. On timing, I'd like everything ready for a final check on Friday so we don't lose the following week.

turns.inner_thought: Friday works. To me that means I should have enough in place to verify the checklist against the manuscript, appendices, and uploaded files, and keep going through the end of the day until the package is actually compliant. Better to use Friday as the true pre-submission validation point.
turns.utterance: Friday works for me. I can use that as the point to verify the checklist against the manuscript, appendices, and uploaded files before submission.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—his checklist pass should flag any missing wording in the draft, which is what I need. I'll focus on the abstract and discussion, keep the narrative sharp, and avoid getting dragged into creating lots of new materials unless something is clearly essential.
turns.utterance: Excellent. I'll tighten the abstract and discussion in the meantime, and then your checklist pass can point us to any missing wording we should patch into the draft.

turns.inner_thought: Once I populate the checklist thoroughly, the remaining supplementary needs should be obvious—search documentation, traceability pieces, maybe a clearer supporting file structure. That will make the PRISMA-compliant submission package genuinely submission-ready rather than just superficially complete.
turns.utterance: Exactly. Once the checklist is populated, it should be pretty easy to see which supplementary pieces are still needed to make the package submission-ready.

turns.inner_thought: So the division is simple: Noah handles the checklist and the flow diagram, I finish the narrative sections, and Friday I do the near-final editorial pass. As long as we're not expanding scope too much, this should keep us on track for submission next week.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. So you'll handle the checklist and the flow diagram, I'll finalize the narrative sections, and then we'll regroup Friday for the final check.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send a cleaned-up PRISMA package draft before Friday with the checklist, the flow diagram, and whatever supporting files I can assemble or flag. If Friday goes the way I expect, we should be able to move straight from compliance review into the submission portal.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll send a cleaned-up PRISMA package draft ahead of Friday so we can move directly into submission once the check is done.
